Empirical Research Plan: “The Private Wealth Returns to Serving in Parliament, 1950-1970”

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Primary method: Sharp Regression Discontinuity Design (RDD) applied to the vote-share margin in each constituency‐election.

Why RDD?
• Treatment (obtaining a seat) is mechanically assigned when the two-party (or two-candidate) vote margin crosses zero.  
• Close winners and close losers are ex-ante similar; assignment around the cutoff is as-good-as-random.  
• Wealth is observed pre- and post-election, letting us estimate both (i) the level effect and (ii) the change in wealth over time.  

Extensions for robustness:  
• Difference-in-Differences on the narrow-margin sample (RD-in-time) to exploit multiple elections per individual.  
• Event-study graphs to show dynamic treatment effects.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control Definitions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  Treated = 1 if candidate i in constituency c at election t wins the seat (first-past-the-post), 0 otherwise.

Control group  
  Candidates who lose the same constituency election.

Running variable and cutoff  
  Running variable mict = (candidate vote-share – highest opponent vote-share) in percentage points.  
  Cutoff = 0. Winning occurs when mict ≥ 0.

Bandwidth  
  Data-driven (Calonico–Cattaneo–Titiunik, 2014) with several symmetric and asymmetric bandwidths tried for robustness (e.g., 2 pp, 3 pp, 5 pp around zero).

Treatment timing / outcomes  
  • Pre-t wealth: last available asset disclosure or estimated net worth dated ≤ 1 year before election t.  
  • Post-t wealth: wealth as of five years after t (or next disclosure), and at the end of parliamentary term.  
  Main outcome: ΔWealthi ≡ ln(Wealthpost) – ln(Wealthpre).  
  Secondary: level of post-t wealth, portfolio composition, real‐estate holdings.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
--------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes: In the absence of treatment, expected wealth trajectories vary smoothly with the vote margin at zero.  
  Plausibility: Votes in Westminster FPTP elections are not manipulable by candidates once ballots are cast; last-minute shocks are essentially random around zero.

A2. No precise sorting/manipulation of the running variable: Candidates cannot systematically shift just enough votes to move from −0.1 pp to +0.1 pp.  
  Plausibility: Post-war UK elections had secret ballots, standardized counts, and rare recount adjustments too small to reflect candidate control.

A3. Stable Composition: Close winners and losers have comparable observables (age, education, prior wealth) right at the cutoff.  
  Plausibility: Testable with balance checks.

A4. SUTVA: One candidate’s victory does not affect another’s private wealth near the cutoff (reasonable at individual level).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigations
--------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Manipulation / recounts at the cutoff  
  • Run McCrary density test; visually inspect histogram of margins.  
  • Exclude constituencies with judicial recounts if any systematic bias is found.

T2. Differential attrition in wealth data (e.g., winners must file disclosure, losers may not)  
  • Compile wealth from external sources (probate records, rich lists) for both groups.  
  • Use inverse-probability weighting or Lee bounds if missingness differs.

T3. Anticipation or pre-trends (rich individuals self-select into winnable marginal seats)  
  • Include pre-election wealth as covariate or focus on ΔWealth.  
  • Check covariate balance (age, occupation, pre-wealth) within each narrow bandwidth.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
--------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # fast lfe-style OLS
library(rdrobust)      # rd estimation and plots
library(rddensity)     # McCrary test
library(broom)         # tidy outputs

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Data Loading
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
elex <- read_csv("uk_elections_1950_1970.csv")          # election results
wealth <- read_csv("candidate_wealth_panel.csv")        # wealth observations

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Merge & Variable Construction
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
df <- elex %>%
  left_join(wealth, by = c("cand_id", "election_year")) %>%
  mutate(
    margin = vote_share - opponent_max_share,          # running variable
    treat  = as.integer(margin >= 0),
    lwealth_pre  = log(wealth_pre),
    lwealth_post = log(wealth_post_5yr),
    d_log_wealth = lwealth_post - lwealth_pre
  ) %>%
  drop_na(margin, d_log_wealth)     # keep complete cases for main spec

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Graphical Diagnostics
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Density test
rddensity(df$margin)
# Bin scatter for covariate balance
ggplot(df, aes(margin, lwealth_pre)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Main RDD Estimation (local linear, robust bias-corrected)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
rd_main <- rdrobust(
  y  = df$d_log_wealth,
  x  = df$margin,
  p  = 1,                 # local linear
  h  = NULL,              # data-driven bandwidth
  covs = df %>% select(age, education_years, lwealth_pre)  # optional
)
summary(rd_main)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Alternative Bandwidth & Polynomial Robustness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
for (bw in c(0.02, 0.03, 0.05)) {     # margins in proportion, i.e. 2-5 pp
  tmp <- rdrobust(df$d_log_wealth, df$margin, h = bw, p = 1)
  print(paste("bw:", bw))
  print(tmp$coef)
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 6. RD-in-Time Difference-in-Differences Robustness
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# Keep candidates observed in multiple elections
panel <- df %>%
  group_by(cand_id) %>%
  mutate(any_win = max(treat)) %>%
  ungroup()

did_rd <- feols(lwealth ~ treat*post + age + education_years |
                          cand_id + election_year,
                data = panel)
etable(did_rd)

# ---------------------------------------------------------------
# 7. Placebo Cutoff Test
# ---------------------------------------------------------------
placebo <- rdrobust(
  y = df$d_log_wealth,
  x = df$margin - 0.05,      # fake cutoff at +5 pp
  h = 0.05
)
summary(placebo)
```

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
--------------------------------------------------------------------
Prior: Winning a seat should raise personal wealth. Salary + pension + access to lucrative post-parliamentary careers (board seats, consulting) plausibly translate into a 10–20 percent higher net worth five years after the election for marginal winners relative to marginal losers.

We also expect heterogeneity: stronger effects for younger, professional-background MPs and for Conservatives (better business networks).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)
(1 = definitely satisfied, 0 = questionable)
--------------------------------------------------------------------
C1  No discontinuity in density of the running variable        … 1  
C2  Covariates smooth at cutoff                               … 1  
C3  Correct functional form / bandwidth robustness            … 1  
C4  No omitted simultaneous treatments at cutoff              … 0.5 (possible recounts)  
C5  Outcome measured consistently for both sides              … 0.5 (disclosure bias)  

Total = 4/5 → method appears highly credible with planned checks.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
This plan lays out a transparent RDD to estimate the private wealth returns to political office in post-war Britain and details diagnostics, robustness, and expected findings.
